newsitem.title: USA: Exxon to refute previous gasoline claims in FTC deal.
newsitem.headline: Exxon to refute previous gasoline claims in FTC deal.

text.p: In a settlement with the Federal Trade Commission, Exxon Corp. has agreed to run a series of advertisements that will take back past claims that using premium gasoline will make cars run more efficiently, the FTC said on Tuesday.
The out-of-court settlement is seen as a landmark case by the FTC, marking the first time a major U.S. oil company will admit in public that most cars need only regular octane gasoline.

"Now the largest oil company in the country will give consumers the straight story. Consumers can save money if they understand that most cars won't run longer, faster, cleaner or better on premium gasoline," said Jodie Bernstein, director of FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection.
However, Exxon said it made no false advertising claims and noted that the FTC has agreed to scientific testing of the engine-cleaning capabilities of high octane fuel.

"The company's participation in this consent agreement is in no way an admission of wrongdoing and that the company maintains there was a sound basis for making its advertising claim," Exxon said in a statement.
Exxon called the agreement, which stems from an FTC lawsuit filed last September, as a "win-win solution" for both sides.
"We had been preparing to challenge the FTC in court over the issue, but our continuing dialogue with the Commission allowed both sides to identify areas of agreement," Exxon said in the statement.
According to the settlement, Exxon will begin running 15-second television advertisements in September in 18 major metropolitan markets, including New York City; Orlando, Fla.; and Dallas.

The ads, carrying the message that most cars will run properly on regular octane gasoline, will be aired for two to three week periods in September and December until it has been determined that 75 percent of the television audience has been reached, said Winston.
Any future claims that octane ratings above 87 assure smoother combustion and efficiency than regular must be backed up by scientific evidence, according to the agreement.
Exxon will also make available information brochures at its 8,700 service stations nationwide.
Despite the settlement, the American love affair with the automobile is likely to continue driving consumers to the higher-priced fuel, analysts said.

"The only way to make a dent in premium gasoline sales is to raise prices prohibitively," said Peter Beutel, president of energy consulting firm Cameron Hanover. "Americans treat their cars like they are pets and will continue to feed them the fancy feast of high octane."
According to the American Automobile Association, fewer than 10 percent of the cars on U.S. roads need premium, although it accounts for more than 20 percent of sales.
Consumers waste $1.7 billion a year on buying premium and the latest AAA survey shows high octane running at a 15-cent premium to regular.
"Maybe the message will finally get through that most cars don't need high priced gasoline," said AAA spokesman Bill Jackman.
For the industry, which argues 19 percent of U.S. cars need premium for better efficiency, sales of high-octane fuel has been an important money earner in tough times.
Traders and analysts say premium earns twice as much in profits as regular and it is unlikely oil companies will give it up anytime soon.
"It would be particularly hard for any refiner to lose a premium outlet," said an economist at a major oil company.
